items.questionAndWhy: Do political labels exaggerate disagreement about the economic system people actually want?
items.whatTheyDid: Across five studies with 1,753 participants, including four preregistered experiments, researchers compared Americans' preferred economic arrangements with the labels they attached to them and tested messages highlighting agreement; a fifth study examined Brazil.
items.whatTheyFound: Across political groups, many preferred a mixture of market arrangements and social protections but described it as capitalist or socialist according to political identity. Highlighting substantive agreement reduced perceived differences and increased reported openness to opposing-party policies and candidates; some effects persisted a month.
items.whatItMeans: Policy preferences and partisan labels are not interchangeable. Demonstrating shared positions can change reported openness in these experimental samples, but does not establish electoral behavior or erase real disagreements.
items.streamTitle: Partisan economic labels obscured shared preferences in US and Brazil
items.streamSummary: Five studies found cross-party support for elements of a mixed economy despite different capitalist/socialist labels. Showing participants the agreement reduced perceived divides and raised stated openness to out-party policies; voting was not measured.

items.questionAndWhy: Are sensation-seeking and impulsivity different ways of responding to uncertain stimulation?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers reanalyzed earlier reward-and-stimulation experiments and ran a preregistered choice task with 527 analyzed UK and US adults. They separately modeled reward, the expected chance of stimulation, uncertainty about stimulation, and choice repetition.
items.whatTheyFound: Higher sensation-seeking was linked to broader sampling and less avoidance of uncertain stimulation; higher impulsivity showed the opposite uncertainty association. Modeling also showed that stimulation value modified those relationships. Some exploratory tests were uncorrected for multiple comparisons.
items.whatItMeans: Do not combine sensation-seeking and impulsivity into one general risk trait. The controlled task isolates computational explanations but does not establish how people behave in gambling, politics, or other real settings.
items.streamTitle: Sensation seeking and impulsivity showed opposite uncertainty patterns
items.streamSummary: A preregistered task with 527 analyzed adults found sensation-seeking related to greater tolerance of uncertain stimulation, whereas impulsivity related to greater avoidance. These model-based patterns need real-world replication.

items.questionAndWhy: Does attention during visual search rely only on a detailed target held in working memory?
items.whatTheyDid: A new review synthesized visual-search findings on working memory, long-term memory, learned regularities, target templates, and active avoidance of distracting objects.
items.whatTheyFound: The reviewed evidence challenges a single-template account: long-term memory, prior selection experience, flexible target representations, and distractor avoidance can all guide attention. This is a synthesis of prior studies, not a new controlled experiment.
items.whatItMeans: Attention models should allow several learned and goal-directed processes to operate together. The review does not provide one universal effect size or show that one mechanism dominates in every setting.
items.streamTitle: Attention during search draws on more than working memory
items.streamSummary: A Nature Reviews Psychology synthesis argues that visual search uses flexible target representations, long-term memory, statistical learning, and distractor avoidance, rather than only a working-memory template.
items.attribution: Carlisle and Woodman — Nature Reviews Psychology (review)

items.questionAndWhy: Can models estimate a learner's changing knowledge by combining response history, concept relationships, and forgetting?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers built MEDKT, joining graph neural networks, a Transformer branch, behavior representations, and a memory-decay component. They evaluated it against comparison models on the ASSIST09, ASSIST12, and Junyi public learning datasets.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors reported small improvements across several prediction metrics on all three datasets, including ROC-AUC gains of 0.81, 0.93, and 1.56 percentage points respectively. F1 on ASSIST09 was a reported exception.
items.whatItMeans: Better retrospective prediction of answers is not proof of better instruction or valid measurement of actual knowledge. Test on new courses, students, and prospective learning outcomes.
items.streamTitle: Knowledge-tracing model improved benchmark prediction, with an F1 exception
items.streamSummary: MEDKT combined behavior history, concept graphs, sequential attention, and modeled forgetting. Three public dataset benchmarks showed small gains on most metrics, while one F1 comparison did not improve.

items.questionAndWhy: What kind of evidence shows that a brain-computer interface decoder will keep working outside its development data?
items.whatTheyDid: A review organized neural-decoding research by the domain held out during evaluation: session, participant, task, device, site, and recording modality. It also distinguished fixed-model transfer from adaptation using target data.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors found that apparently strong development accuracy often does not survive changed users, equipment, or circumstances. The paper proposes reporting standards and prospective tests; it does not introduce a validated universal decoder.
items.whatItMeans: A held-out test from a new participant is not the same as a test on new hardware or over time. Practical benefit also requires assessing calibration burden, maintenance, risks, and sustained function.
items.streamTitle: Brain-computer interface review puts generalization ahead of peak accuracy
items.streamSummary: A new review argues that neural decoding must be tested across sessions, participants, tasks, hardware, and clinical conditions. High development scores alone do not establish durable clinical use.
items.attribution: Gu et al. — npj Biomedical Innovations (review)

items.questionAndWhy: Can prior causal structure help jointly estimate coastal water conditions from different sensor sources?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers proposed a causally informed learning framework that incorporates structural assumptions while combining observations from satellites and autonomous underwater gliders to model coastal marine variables.
items.whatTheyFound: The study presents a tested modeling approach to multimodal environmental estimation. Its assumed structure and fitted relationships are not independent experimental proof of the actual causal network, and transfer beyond the study environment is uncertain.
items.whatItMeans: A useful design pattern is to make prior structural assumptions explicit when fusing sparse observations. Model fit and simulated causal interpretation should remain separate from intervention validation.
items.streamTitle: Causally informed model combines satellite and underwater measurements
items.streamSummary: A new marine-water-quality framework integrates prior structural assumptions with satellite and glider observations. It offers a modeling method, not experimental confirmation of the inferred causal structure.
items.attribution: Hashemi, Mahjouri and Nikoo — Scientific Reports

items.questionAndWhy: How can security policymakers create shared definitions of military and security AI without imposing a single contested interpretation?
items.whatTheyDid: UNIDIR convened an October 23 UN First Committee side event and described its 2026–2027 multidisciplinary effort to develop an AI security lexicon addressing technical terms, political differences, and definitional capture.
items.whatTheyFound: The initiative sets out an expert process and planned reference resource. The announcement does not establish an agreed lexicon, adoption by governments, or measurable improvements in policy coordination.
items.whatItMeans: Shared terminology could reduce avoidable confusion in doctrine, procurement, and governance, but competing definitions should be documented transparently rather than erased.
items.streamTitle: UNIDIR starts a 2026–27 AI security lexicon initiative
items.streamSummary: UNIDIR outlined a multidisciplinary effort to clarify AI security terminology for policymakers, including contested definitions. The October 23 event and plan are not evidence that agreement or adoption has occurred.
items.attribution: UNIDIR — official AI security lexicon event

items.questionAndWhy: How is the US Army expanding access to AI tools for command-and-control and intelligence workflows?
items.whatTheyDid: Striveworks announced on October 22 that its Pentagon enterprise contracting ceiling had increased from $70 million to $700 million over five years, alongside agreements involving Next Generation Command and Control and intelligence workflows.
items.whatTheyFound: The announcement indicates expanded contracting capacity and described deployment plans. The $700 million figure is a contract ceiling, not confirmed spending, and the company did not publish controlled evidence that the tools improved combat outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: Procurement scale signals priority, not delivered capability. Track obligations, integration, operator adoption, audited accuracy, and human authorization requirements separately.
items.streamTitle: Army AI supplier announced a $700 million enterprise contract ceiling
items.streamSummary: Striveworks said its enterprise agreement grew tenfold and would support more Army AI deployments. The headline figure is a ceiling, not funds spent or independently verified mission improvement.

items.questionAndWhy: Can structured AI patient simulations support clinical communication practice as effectively as actor-based training?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers assessed 350 AI-generated consultations across five language models, examined 155 live student consultations, and ran a three-arm randomized pilot with 58 analyzed students comparing AI-patient practice, human actors, and control.
items.whatTheyFound: In the pilot, all groups improved and differences in objective clinical-exam gains were not statistically significant. AI trainees showed the largest numerical self-efficacy gains, but the exploratory advantage did not survive multiple-comparison correction. This was not a definitive equivalence trial.
items.whatItMeans: The architecture can support repeatable practice and diagnostic analysis of missed questions, but a small pilot with retesting effects cannot establish equal effectiveness or patient-care benefit.
items.streamTitle: AI patient-simulator pilot found no clear skill advantage over alternatives
items.streamSummary: A multi-stage study evaluated 350 scripted encounters, 155 live student interactions, and a 58-person randomized pilot. Exam gains did not differ significantly by training arm; equivalence was not demonstrated.
items.attribution: Wu et al. — npj Digital Medicine

items.questionAndWhy: Do AI, peer, and teacher comments influence students' ability to evaluate and use feedback differently?
items.whatTheyDid: A ten-week quasi-experimental study compared three intact Chinese university classes totaling 126 second-language writers. Researchers used pre/post feedback-literacy questionnaires and follow-up interviews.
items.whatTheyFound: The AI and peer-feedback classes improved significantly on some questionnaire dimensions; the teacher-feedback class showed no significant dimension-level change. Groups were intact rather than independently randomized, and the study did not establish durable writing-performance improvements.
items.whatItMeans: Different feedback sources may support different learner skills. The null teacher-group finding is not proof that teachers are ineffective; course and group differences limit causal claims.
items.streamTitle: AI and peer feedback improved some feedback-literacy measures in a classroom study
items.streamSummary: Across 126 students in three intact classes, AI and peer feedback coincided with gains on some self-reported feedback-literacy dimensions; the teacher group showed no significant changes. Assignment was not randomized.
items.attribution: Yan and Meng — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
